title: What causes a CloudFormation stack to get stuck in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` (a resource unreachable / manually modified / insufficient rollback permissions), and how do you recover (fix the resource, then `continue-update-rollback`, optionally skipping specific resources)?
shortTitle: CloudFormation stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED — causes and recovery

s1_definition.profdef: `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` is a terminal-ish CloudFormation stack state that occurs when a stack update fails, CloudFormation attempts to roll the stack back to its last known good configuration, and that rollback itself fails. The stack is now stuck: you cannot run a new update until the rollback is resolved. The usual root causes are that a resource became unreachable or was manually modified outside CloudFormation (so the real state no longer matches what CloudFormation recorded), the deployment role lacks the permissions needed to perform the rollback actions, or a resource genuinely cannot return to its previous state. Recovery is to fix the underlying resource or permission problem and then call `continue-update-rollback`, optionally supplying `ResourcesToSkip` so CloudFormation skips the specific resources it cannot reconcile.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India is renovating a branch using a strict blueprint system (CloudFormation). You submit a change — "move the vault and add a counter." Halfway through, the new vault installation fails. The blueprint system says, "no problem, I'll put everything back the way it was." But when it tries to restore the old vault, it discovers someone had already manually bricked over the old vault doorway without telling the blueprint system. Now the system is stuck: it cannot finish the renovation and it cannot restore the original, because reality no longer matches its records. To get unstuck, a human has to physically fix the doorway (fix the resource) or tell the system "just skip the vault, I'll handle it manually" (skip the resource), and then say "okay, continue putting the rest back" (continue-update-rollback).
s1_definition.oneliner: `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` means the update failed AND the automatic undo also failed — you must fix or skip the offending resource, then run `continue-update-rollback`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` is a terminal-ish CloudFormation stack state that occurs when a stack update fails, CloudFormation attempts to roll the stack back to its last known good configuration, and that rollback itself fails. The stack is now stuck: you cannot run a new update until the rollback is resolved. The usual root causes are that a resource became unreachable or was manually modified outside CloudFormation (so the real state no longer matches what CloudFormation recorded), the deployment role lacks the permissions needed to perform the rollback actions, or a resource genuinely cannot return to its previous state. Recovery is to fix the underlying resource or permission problem and then call `continue-update-rollback`, optionally supplying `ResourcesToSkip` so CloudFormation skips the specific resources it cannot reconcile.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India is renovating a branch using a strict blueprint system (CloudFormation). You submit a change — "move the vault and add a counter." Halfway through, the new vault installation fails. The blueprint system says, "no problem, I'll put everything back the way it was." But when it tries to restore the old vault, it discovers someone had already manually bricked over the old vault doorway without telling the blueprint system. Now the system is stuck: it cannot finish the renovation and it cannot restore the original, because reality no longer matches its records. To get unstuck, a human has to physically fix the doorway (fix the resource) or tell the system "just skip the vault, I'll handle it manually" (skip the resource), and then say "okay, continue putting the rest back" (continue-update-rollback).

**One line to remember:** `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` means the update failed AND the automatic undo also failed — you must fix or skip the offending resource, then run `continue-update-rollback`.

sections.s2_technical:
CloudFormation manages infrastructure as a stack, and it keeps an internal record of the expected state of every resource. When you submit an update, CloudFormation computes the difference and applies it. If any resource in the update fails, CloudFormation does not leave the stack half-changed; it automatically begins a rollback to the last stable state, moving the stack into `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_IN_PROGRESS`. If that rollback completes, the stack lands in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` and you can try again. The problem state is `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED`, which means the rollback itself could not finish.

There are three common root causes. The first is drift: someone modified or deleted a resource manually in the console or CLI, so when CloudFormation tries to restore the previous configuration, the resource is not in the state CloudFormation expected. A classic example is a security group rule or an RDS parameter that was hand-edited; CloudFormation tries to put back its recorded version and the operation fails because the dependency chain no longer holds. The second cause is a resource that is genuinely unreachable or stuck — for instance an EC2 instance that will not stop, an Auto Scaling group that cannot reach capacity, or a Lambda that keeps failing a custom-resource response so CloudFormation waits and then times out. The third cause is insufficient permissions: the IAM role CloudFormation uses to act on your behalf (the service role, or your own credentials if no service role is set) lacks a permission needed for the rollback action, such as deleting a resource it created during the failed update.

The recovery path is deliberate. First you diagnose: open the stack events and find the specific resource whose status is `UPDATE_FAILED` or whose rollback failed, and read the status reason, which usually names the exact problem. Then you fix the underlying cause out of band — restore the manually modified resource to a sane state, unstick the resource, or add the missing IAM permission to the deployment role. Once the real-world problem is resolved, you call `continue-update-rollback`, which tells CloudFormation to retry the rollback from where it stopped. If a particular resource simply cannot be reconciled — for example a resource that was deleted outside CloudFormation and cannot be recreated during a rollback — you pass `--resources-to-skip` with that resource's logical ID. CloudFormation then abandons trying to roll that one resource back, marks it skipped, and completes the rollback for everything else, landing the stack in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE`.

The senior-level nuances matter in a bank. Skipping a resource is not free: after a skip, CloudFormation's record of that resource is out of sync with reality, so you must reconcile it afterward, often by importing the resource or correcting it in a subsequent change set, otherwise the next update can fail again. You also prevent this state in the first place: enable termination protection and change-set reviews, forbid manual console edits to CloudFormation-managed resources (drift is the number-one cause), use an explicit least-privilege service role so you control exactly what CloudFormation can do, and run `detect-drift` before large updates so you catch manual changes before they turn a routine update into a stuck rollback. Nested stacks add a wrinkle: a parent can be stuck because a child stack is stuck, so you resolve the child first.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the payments platform is deployed entirely through CloudFormation. Rajesh, a software engineer, submits an update to the payments stack to resize the database and tighten a security group. The deployment team repeatedly hits stuck rollbacks, and we want to model exactly why and how to recover, because in a bank you cannot just delete and recreate a production stack holding live account data.

Problem 1 — During an earlier incident, an on-call engineer manually edited the payments security group in the console to open a port quickly. CloudFormation never recorded that change. Now Rajesh's update fails on an unrelated resource, CloudFormation tries to roll the security group back to its recorded version, and the rollback fails because the live group no longer matches. This is drift, and it is the single most common cause of `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED`.

Problem 2 — The deployment role was created with narrow permissions and is missing `ec2:DeleteSecurityGroupRule`. When CloudFormation tries to undo a rule it added during the failed update, it is denied, and the rollback fails. This is the insufficient-permissions cause.

Problem 3 — One resource, an S3 bucket, was deleted entirely outside CloudFormation during cleanup. CloudFormation cannot roll it back to its previous state because it no longer exists and cannot be recreated in a rollback. This resource must be skipped.

The code models a tiny CloudFormation-like engine so the state machine and recovery are explicit. We build `StackResource` (a resource with a status and a flag for whether it was manually modified or deleted), a `Stack` that holds resources and a `StackStatus`, and a `CloudFormationEngine` that performs `update`, automatic `rollback`, diagnosis, and `continueUpdateRollback(resourcesToSkip)`. The demo drives a stack into `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` three different ways, then recovers it by fixing drift, granting permission, and skipping the deleted bucket.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -jar target/cfn-recovery-service-1.0.0.jar

# The real AWS CLI equivalent of the recovery:
# 1. Inspect why it is stuck:
aws cloudformation describe-stack-events --stack-name bank-payments \
  --query "StackEvents[?ResourceStatus=='UPDATE_FAILED']"

# 2. Fix drift / permissions out of band (console or CLI), then continue,
#    skipping the resource that cannot be reconciled:
aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback \
  --stack-name bank-payments \
  --resources-to-skip PaymentsArchiveBucket

# 3. Confirm recovery:
aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name bank-payments \
  --query "Stacks[0].StackStatus"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the `bank-payments` stack with three resources — a security group that was manually modified (drift), a database whose rollback is blocked by a missing IAM permission, and an archive bucket that was deleted outside CloudFormation.

Step 1: Rajesh submits an update. The engine sets the stack to `UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS`. The update fails on `PaymentsDatabase`.

Step 2: CloudFormation automatically begins rollback, setting `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_IN_PROGRESS`. It walks every resource and asks "can you roll back?" The security group says no (drift), the database says no (no permission), the bucket says no (deleted). Three blockers.

Step 3: Because there are blockers, the stack lands in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED`. It is now stuck; no new update can run.

Step 4: The engineer runs diagnosis, which reads the stack events and prints each blocker with its exact reason — drift, missing permission, deleted resource.

Step 5: The team fixes the fixable causes out of band. They reconcile the drifted security group so its live state matches the recorded state, and they add the missing permission to the deploy role. The bucket is gone permanently and cannot be recreated during a rollback, so it will be skipped.

Step 6: The engineer calls `continueUpdateRollback` with `PaymentsArchiveBucket` in the skip set. CloudFormation retries, skips the bucket (logging that it must be reconciled later), finds the security group and database now roll back cleanly, and completes. The stack lands in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE`.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-25 03:40:00 INFO    Update started on stack bank-payments
2026-10-25 03:40:00 SEVERE  Resource PaymentsDatabase failed to update — starting rollback
2026-10-25 03:40:00 SEVERE  Rollback FAILED for PaymentsSecurityGroup: resource drifted — live state != recorded state
2026-10-25 03:40:00 SEVERE  Rollback FAILED for PaymentsDatabase: deploy role lacks permission for rollback action
2026-10-25 03:40:00 SEVERE  Rollback FAILED for PaymentsArchiveBucket: resource deleted outside CloudFormation
2026-10-25 03:40:00 SEVERE  Stack bank-payments is STUCK in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED (3 blocker(s))
2026-10-25 03:40:00 INFO    Stack status now: UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED
2026-10-25 03:40:00 WARNING SKIPPING PaymentsArchiveBucket — must reconcile manually afterwards
2026-10-25 03:40:00 INFO    continue-update-rollback succeeded — stack is UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE
2026-10-25 03:40:00 INFO    Final stack status: UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
`UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` happens when a CloudFormation stack update fails, CloudFormation automatically tries to roll the stack back to its last stable configuration, and that rollback itself cannot finish. The stack is then stuck — you cannot run a new update until you resolve the rollback. In my experience the three causes are almost always drift, permissions, or a genuinely unreconcilable resource. Drift means someone modified or deleted a resource manually outside CloudFormation, so when CloudFormation tries to restore its recorded version the live state no longer matches and the operation fails. Permissions means the deployment role lacks a right needed to perform a rollback action, like deleting a resource CloudFormation created during the failed update. And sometimes a resource simply cannot return to its previous state, for example because it was deleted entirely and cannot be recreated during a rollback.

The recovery is deliberate rather than a retry button. First I diagnose by reading the stack events and finding the resource whose status is `UPDATE_FAILED` along with its status reason, which usually names the exact problem. Then I fix the underlying cause out of band: I reconcile the drifted resource so its live state matches what CloudFormation recorded, or I add the missing permission to the deployment role, or I unstick the resource. Once the real-world problem is resolved I call `continue-update-rollback`, which retries the rollback from where it stopped. If a specific resource cannot be reconciled at all, I pass that resource's logical ID in `--resources-to-skip`, and CloudFormation abandons rolling that one resource back, marks it skipped, and completes the rollback for everything else, landing the stack in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE`.

The nuance I always call out is that skipping is not a clean fix. After a skip, CloudFormation's record of that resource is out of sync with reality, so I have to reconcile it afterwards — usually by importing the resource or correcting it in a later change set — otherwise the next update can fail the same way. And for nested stacks, a parent can be stuck only because a child stack is stuck, so I resolve the child first.

At the National Bank of India this came up on our payments stack, and the root cause was classic drift: during an incident an on-call engineer had hand-edited a security group in the console, CloudFormation never recorded it, and a later routine update failed its rollback trying to restore the recorded version. We also had a case where the deployment role was missing a permission to delete a rule it had added. We recovered by reconciling the security group and adding the permission, then running `continue-update-rollback`, and we skipped exactly one resource — an archive bucket that had been deleted outside CloudFormation — which we later re-imported. The lasting fix was prevention: we forbade manual console edits to CloudFormation-managed resources, ran drift detection before large updates, and gave CloudFormation an explicit least-privilege service role, because in a bank you cannot simply tear down and recreate a production stack holding live account data.
